events.text:
Here is the comparison, with citations to the sources.

## Direct answer

Britannica (1771–1797) treats "inflammable air" in coal mines under the "Damps" entry: it is a gas generated in the bowels of the earth (per Dr. Priestley, made of "elementary fire, charcoal or phlogiston and stable water"), supplied by coal's phlogiston plus underground heat and water, which collects in pockets and explodes with force "equal to that of gun powder" if a workman enters with a candle; the remedy is to burn it off safely (a man lies flat and holds a lighted candle on a pole to "free the mine from a troublesome guest") or, where too much has accumulated, to ventilate the mine through shafts to create "a constant current of air."

Wikipedia (Firedamp) defines it as "any flammable gas found in coal mines, typically coalbed methane," which accumulates in pockets in coal and adjacent strata and explodes when penetrated; it groups it with blackdamp, whitedamp, stinkdamp (hydrogen sulfide), and afterdamp under the collective term "damp," and traces the name to Old English *fyr* / proto-Germanic *fūr* ("fire").

## Evidence

**Britannica [B:1214:0]** — entry "Damps" (p. 638), passage about inflammable air in mines:
- "Dr Priestley has shown, that inflammable air is comprised of pure elementary fire, charcoal or phlogiston and stable water; and that this composition may take place even in water."
- "All the materials are to be met with in the bowels of the earth. Coal ... is abundantly able to supply the phlogiston; the natural motions of the earth affords water, and the heat ... in the bowels of the earth, may be sufficient to produce a quantity of inflammable air."
- An explosion's force was "equal to that of gun powder," occasioned by workmen going down with lighted candles.
- Prevention: "by letting fire to it" — the inflammable air, "being much lighter than any other kind, will naturally rise to the top so that a man, lying flat on the ground to avoid the force of the explosion, and holding up a lighted candle fixed upon a pole, ... free the mine from a troublesome guest"; otherwise "the method commonly adopted is to produce a constant circulation of air ... through all parts of the mine" via a perpendicular opening "which they call a shaft."

OCR note: the Britannica text is raw 18th-century OCR (long "s" read as "f", e.g. "infammake," "Priefley," "vason," "phogililon"), so I quote only the verified reading and checked it against the page scan (row 1214, image sha256 17d180a9…).

**Wikipedia [W:505455:1345728236] — "Firedamp":**
- "Firedamp is any flammable gas found in coal mines, typically coalbed methane. ... The gas accumulates in pockets in the coal and adjacent strata and, when they are penetrated, the release of the gas can cause explosions."
- "Damp is the collective name given to all gases (other than air) found in coal mines in Great Britain and North America," including blackdamp, whitedamp, stinkdamp, and afterdamp.
- Name derives via Old English *fyr* and proto-Germanic *fūr* for "fire."

## What changed (inference)

Inference: the knowledge changed, not just the words. Britannica explains inflammable air through the obsolete phlogiston theory (Priestley; elementary fire + phlogiston from coal + stable water, generated by underground heat), while Wikipedia identifies firedamp as methane (coalbed methane). The language also shifted: "inflammable air" / "damps" became "firedamp," and the cure moved from burning the gas off with a hand-held candle to ventilation and (later) safety lamps such as the Davy lamp (1815).

## Uncertainty

The Britannica↔Wikipedia pairing here is **uncertain**: `get_pair` returned status `no_clear_counterpart` with rerank logit -4.46 and margin 0.48, so the link to Wikipedia "Firedamp" is the best candidate kept for review, not a confirmed saved pair, and no saved comparison/drift block exists for it. Also, the Britannica passage text was truncated at the end, and the OCR contains errors (noted above), so treat quotations as close readings verified against the scan where legible, not as perfect transcripts.

final_text:
Here is the comparison, with citations to the sources.

## Direct answer

Britannica (1771–1797) treats "inflammable air" in coal mines under the "Damps" entry: it is a gas generated in the bowels of the earth (per Dr. Priestley, made of "elementary fire, charcoal or phlogiston and stable water"), supplied by coal's phlogiston plus underground heat and water, which collects in pockets and explodes with force "equal to that of gun powder" if a workman enters with a candle; the remedy is to burn it off safely (a man lies flat and holds a lighted candle on a pole to "free the mine from a troublesome guest") or, where too much has accumulated, to ventilate the mine through shafts to create "a constant current of air."

Wikipedia (Firedamp) defines it as "any flammable gas found in coal mines, typically coalbed methane," which accumulates in pockets in coal and adjacent strata and explodes when penetrated; it groups it with blackdamp, whitedamp, stinkdamp (hydrogen sulfide), and afterdamp under the collective term "damp," and traces the name to Old English *fyr* / proto-Germanic *fūr* ("fire").

## Evidence

**Britannica [B:1214:0]** — entry "Damps" (p. 638), passage about inflammable air in mines:
- "Dr Priestley has shown, that inflammable air is comprised of pure elementary fire, charcoal or phlogiston and stable water; and that this composition may take place even in water."
- "All the materials are to be met with in the bowels of the earth. Coal ... is abundantly able to supply the phlogiston; the natural motions of the earth affords water, and the heat ... in the bowels of the earth, may be sufficient to produce a quantity of inflammable air."
- An explosion's force was "equal to that of gun powder," occasioned by workmen going down with lighted candles.
- Prevention: "by letting fire to it" — the inflammable air, "being much lighter than any other kind, will naturally rise to the top so that a man, lying flat on the ground to avoid the force of the explosion, and holding up a lighted candle fixed upon a pole, ... free the mine from a troublesome guest"; otherwise "the method commonly adopted is to produce a constant circulation of air ... through all parts of the mine" via a perpendicular opening "which they call a shaft."

OCR note: the Britannica text is raw 18th-century OCR (long "s" read as "f", e.g. "infammake," "Priefley," "vason," "phogililon"), so I quote only the verified reading and checked it against the page scan (row 1214, image sha256 17d180a9…).

**Wikipedia [W:505455:1345728236] — "Firedamp":**
- "Firedamp is any flammable gas found in coal mines, typically coalbed methane. ... The gas accumulates in pockets in the coal and adjacent strata and, when they are penetrated, the release of the gas can cause explosions."
- "Damp is the collective name given to all gases (other than air) found in coal mines in Great Britain and North America," including blackdamp, whitedamp, stinkdamp, and afterdamp.
- Name derives via Old English *fyr* and proto-Germanic *fūr* for "fire."

## What changed (inference)

Inference: the knowledge changed, not just the words. Britannica explains inflammable air through the obsolete phlogiston theory (Priestley; elementary fire + phlogiston from coal + stable water, generated by underground heat), while Wikipedia identifies firedamp as methane (coalbed methane). The language also shifted: "inflammable air" / "damps" became "firedamp," and the cure moved from burning the gas off with a hand-held candle to ventilation and (later) safety lamps such as the Davy lamp (1815).

## Uncertainty

The Britannica↔Wikipedia pairing here is **uncertain**: `get_pair` returned status `no_clear_counterpart` with rerank logit -4.46 and margin 0.48, so the link to Wikipedia "Firedamp" is the best candidate kept for review, not a confirmed saved pair, and no saved comparison/drift block exists for it. Also, the Britannica passage text was truncated at the end, and the OCR contains errors (noted above), so treat quotations as close readings verified against the scan where legible, not as perfect transcripts.
